_about: Queue for the weekly story writer. Take topics from the top whose slug has no prototype/sketch_<slug>/ folder yet. Facts listed here were checked; anything you add must be verified with a web search and cited in story.json sources. Prefer the hedged wording given here.

queue.title: The Bystander Effect (Darley & Latane, 1968)
queue.angle: You hear someone having a seizure over an intercom. Do you go?
facts: 1964, New York: the murder of Kitty Genovese; the New York Times reported 38 witnesses who did nothing.
Later reporting (incl. the NYT itself, 2016) found the 38-witnesses story was exaggerated: fewer saw the attack, and some did call or help.
Darley & Latane (1968): students talked over an intercom; one (an actor, on tape) seemed to have a seizure.
When participants thought they were the only listener, about 85% went for help before the seizure ended; with four others listening, about 31%.
Lesson: the more people present, the less responsible each one feels (diffusion of responsibility).
queue.twist: The famous 38 witnesses were exaggerated, but the lab result held: a crowd makes each person less likely to act.
queue.ending_question: If you're one of many, will you be the one who moves?
sources: Darley, J. M., & Latane, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies. JPSP 8(4).
New York Times editor's note on the Genovese story (2016).

queue.title: Little Albert (Watson & Rayner, 1920)
queue.angle: You are a 9-month-old baby who loves a white rat. Then a loud bang starts every time you touch it.
facts: 1920, Johns Hopkins: John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner studied a 9-month-old boy called 'Albert B.'
At first Albert showed no fear of a white rat, a rabbit, a dog, masks or cotton wool.
Whenever he reached for the rat, they struck a steel bar with a hammer behind his head; he startled and cried.
After repeated pairings he cried at the rat alone, and the fear spread to similar things: a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat, a Santa Claus mask.
He left the study before any attempt to remove the fear; who he was later is still debated.
queue.twist: Fear can be learned in days, and the researchers never undid it. Today this study is a lesson in research ethics.
queue.ending_question: Which of your fears did you learn, and could you unlearn it?
sources: Watson, J. B., & Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. J Experimental Psychology 3(1).

queue.title: The Marshmallow Test (Mischel, 1960s-70s)
queue.angle: You are four. One marshmallow now, or two if you can wait alone in a room.
facts: Walter Mischel's studies at Stanford's Bing Nursery School: a child could eat one treat now, or get two by waiting (up to about 15-20 minutes) alone.
Some children waited by distracting themselves: covering their eyes, singing, turning away.
Follow-ups years later linked longer waiting to better outcomes such as higher SAT scores.
A larger 2018 replication (Watts, Duncan & Quan) found the link was much smaller, and mostly explained by family background and early ability.
queue.twist: Waiting wasn't pure willpower: it was also about trust and circumstances. Kids who had reason to trust the adult waited longer (Kidd et al., 2013).
queue.ending_question: Is it willpower, or do you just not trust that the second marshmallow will come?
sources: Mischel, W., Shoda, Y., & Rodriguez, M. L. (1989). Delay of gratification in children. Science 244.
Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., & Quan, H. (2018). Psychological Science 29(7).
Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking. Cognition 126(1).

queue.title: Robbers Cave (Sherif, 1954)
queue.angle: You're 11, at a summer camp. You don't know there's another group of boys across the woods.
facts: 1954, Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma: Muzafer Sherif's study with 22 eleven- and twelve-year-old boys split into two groups.
The groups named themselves the Eagles and the Rattlers.
Competitions (tug-of-war, games with prizes) quickly turned into name-calling, flag burning and cabin raids.
Shared problems that needed both groups (a broken water supply, a stuck truck) brought them back together.
queue.twist: Contact alone didn't fix the hate. Working together on a shared goal did.
queue.ending_question: Who is your 'other group', and what goal could you share?
sources: Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., & Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup Conflict and Cooperation: The Robbers Cave Experiment.

queue.title: Phineas Gage (1848)
queue.angle: You're a railroad foreman. An iron rod is about to go through your head, and you'll survive.
facts: 1848, Vermont: railroad foreman Phineas Gage was packing explosive powder with an iron rod when it went off.
The rod, over a metre long, shot up through his left cheek and out the top of his skull, damaging the front of his brain.
He survived, could talk and walk; his doctor, John Harlow, later wrote that friends said he was 'no longer Gage'.
Later he worked for years, including as a stagecoach driver in Chile, suggesting he partly recovered.
queue.twist: The famous 'he became a monster' story grew over time. His later life suggests the brain can adapt.
queue.ending_question: If your personality can change with your brain, who is the real you?
sources: Harlow, J. M. (1868). Recovery from the passage of an iron bar through the head.
Macmillan, M. (2000). An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage.

queue.title: Patient H.M. (1953)
queue.angle: You wake up after surgery. From now on, every new person you meet is a stranger, forever.
facts: 1953: Henry Molaison had surgery removing parts of both medial temporal lobes (including much of the hippocampus) to stop severe epilepsy.
Afterwards he could not form new long-term memories of events and facts.
Psychologist Brenda Milner studied him for decades; he met her many times but did not remember her.
Yet he got better at a mirror-drawing task day after day, without remembering ever doing it.
queue.twist: Memory isn't one thing: his hands learned what his mind could not remember.
queue.ending_question: What do you remember with your body that your mind has forgotten?
sources: Scoville, W. B., & Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions.

queue.title: The Bobo Doll (Bandura, 1961)
queue.angle: You're a small child watching an adult hit a big inflatable clown. Then they leave you alone with it.
facts: 1961, Stanford: Albert Bandura's study with children aged about 3 to 6.
Some children watched an adult punch, kick and shout at an inflatable Bobo doll; others watched a calm adult.
Left alone with toys, children who saw aggression copied it, often the exact moves and words.
Children who watched the calm adult were much less aggressive.
queue.twist: Nobody told them to hit. They learned it just by watching.
queue.ending_question: Who is watching you, and what are they learning?
sources: Bandura, A., Ross, D., & Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. J Abnormal & Social Psychology 63(3).

queue.title: The Pygmalion Effect (Rosenthal & Jacobson, 1968)
queue.angle: Your teacher has just been told you're about to 'bloom'. You have no idea.
facts: 1960s, a California elementary school: researchers gave students a test and told teachers some children were about to 'bloom' intellectually.
Those children were actually picked at random.
By the end of the year, the 'bloomers' in the youngest grades showed bigger IQ gains than their classmates.
Later research found the effect is real but usually smaller than the original study suggested.
queue.twist: Nothing changed in the children: only in what the teacher expected.
queue.ending_question: Whose expectations are you living up to, or down to?
sources: Rosenthal, R., & Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom.
Jussim, L., & Harber, K. D. (2005). Teacher expectations and self-fulfilling prophecies. PSPR 9(2).
